To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) we have developed a fragment-based method for the design of RNA sequences; (ii) we have developed an efficient weighted sampling algorithm for the design of large RNA sequences; (iii) we have developed the first web server for the design of synthetic and natural RNA sequences.
We present a novel web-server, incaRNAfBinV, for fragment based design of RNA sequences that incorporates biological information.

the design of novel RNA sequences that fold into a given target secondary structure.
the inverse RNA folding design problem, where the input is a target RNA secondary and the output is a sequence that folds into the given structure.
the inverse RNA folding, i.e., the design of sequences which fold into a given RNA structure and the detection of novel RNA sequences that fold into a given structure.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a web server for designing synthetic RNA sequences, which can be used for various applications.

the web server incaRNAtin provides the most comprehensive and flexible solution to date for the design of RNA sequences, and incaRNAfbiinv provides an alternative approach for the design of regulatory RNA sequences.

we developed a novel fragment-based design approach for RNA sequences, which allows the design of RNA sequences with a high degree of sequence similarity to natural sequences and which are not necessarily exact solutions of the inverse folding problem.
The main takeaway from our work is that

RNAfbinv, the fragment-based design approach, and incaRNAs are all available in a single web server, incaRNAfbi, which can be used as an interactive tool for the design of synthetic RNA molecules and for the detection of natural occurring RNA molecules.
the fragment-based design approach of RNAfbinv is able to generate sequences that fold into target secondary structures with high accuracy, even if the target is not exactly folded.
the fragment-based design approach is more robust than the conventional one and is capable of designing RNA sequences with higher target similarity.
